title: An integer congruent to 3 modulo 4 is not a sum of two squares
statement: For every integer n with n = 3 (mod 4) there are no integers a, b with n = a^2 + b^2. This is ADR-0603's boundary-refutation grade of the two-squares family: it is the exact complement of the residue condition in Fermat's theorem, and it is CHEAP where the theorem is expensive, needing no descent and no ordering argument at all. The supporting statement is Int.sq_modEq_four_zero_or_one -- every integer square is 0 or 1 modulo 4.

notes: The parity split needed NO new Int-level parity lemma: Int.Even n is DEFINED as Nat.Even (natAbs n) in int_prelude/parity.rs, so Nat.even_or_odd_exists read at natAbs a already IS the Int dichotomy, up to one delta unfold the kernel does for free. Each branch writes a as 2k or 2k+1 with the DEFINABLE witness k := a/2 (Int.ediv_two_mul_two_of_even and Int.ediv_two_mul_two_add_one_of_odd), so no existential is opened. The residue is read off with Int.modEq_add_mul_left, which is unconditional in the modulus, so no 0 < 4 side condition appears anywhere. The four leaves close by REDUCTION and not by any inequality: ModEq 4 3 r unfolds to Eq Int (emod 3 4) (emod r 4) with both sides closed numerals, and Int.emod is a structural Int.rec/Nat.rec definition, so the kernel computes them; Int.natAbs injectivity plus Nat.ne_of_beq_eq_false finishes. The negative half of the battery is what makes the positive half a measurement: 4, 5, 13 and 17 are each confirmed NOT to admit the refutation, and 5, 13, 17 are exactly the primes the sibling fact witnesses.
